content: The analysis of data comparing decentralized and centralized care for tuberculosis (TB) patients revealed that decentralized care improved treatment success rates and reduced loss to follow-up. However, the risk of death and treatment failure showed minimal differences between the two approaches. Limited data were available on adverse reactions, adherence, acquired drug resistance, and costs. Both HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals were included in the studies, but the data were not stratified by HIV status. Concerns were raised about potential bias, as healthcare workers may have selected patients with worse prognoses for centralized care, and none of the studies controlled for this risk. Decentralized care may not be suitable for patients with severe TB, highly infectious forms of the disease, serious comorbidities, or those with adherence challenges. Hospitalization should remain an option when appropriate, and this review did not include patients requiring surgical care. Cost-effectiveness modeling showed that outpatient-based care was generally less expensive than inpatient care in most settings, with cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted being lower in outpatient models in over 90% of cases. However, costs varied widely depending on the healthcare setting and non-drug-related expenses. Decentralized care was associated with reduced resource use and comparable mortality prevention among primary and secondary cases compared to hospitalization. However, the outcomes of some studies on ambulatory care may have been suboptimal due to the use of older, less effective treatment regimens. Placing patients on effective therapy is expected to reduce bacterial load and transmission of drug-resistant TB. National TB programs should consider reallocating resources from hospital-based to ambulatory care models, ensuring adequate infrastructure, training, and support for decentralized care. Patient preferences should be prioritized when choosing between centralized and decentralized care. Decentralized care for MDR-TB patients requires robust treatment supervision, patient education, social support, staff training, infection control practices, and quality assurance. While cost estimates varied widely, decentralized care was generally found to be cost-effective. The financial benefits include earlier treatment initiation, preventing severe illness, and reducing TB transmission. However, legal and regulatory barriers in some regions may restrict decentralized treatment, particularly for injectable therapies. For children and adolescents exposed to or diagnosed with TB, decentralized and family-centered care models are recommended to improve case detection and access to TB preventive treatment (TPT). Pediatric TB services are often centralized at higher levels of care, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment. Decentralization and integration of TB services into primary healthcare (PHC) can address these gaps, especially in high-burden settings. Family-centered care, which considers the needs and preferences of the child and family, can enhance treatment adherence and outcomes. Studies showed that strengthening diagnostic capacity at the PHC level and improving community-facility linkages increased case notifications and TPT initiation. Family-centered care, including socioeconomic support for affected families, was associated with improved TPT initiation and completion. However, evidence on the specific impact of these models on pediatric TB outcomes remains limited. The implementation of decentralized and family-centered care requires adequate training of healthcare workers, infrastructure development, and community engagement. Active contact investigation at the community and household levels is critical for enhancing case detection and TPT provision. Task-shifting within the healthcare system, supported by training and capacity-building, can further facilitate decentralized care. Adolescents with TB may require different interventions than younger children due to their disease presentation and health-seeking behaviors. Decentralized and integrated care approaches can improve equity, cost-effectiveness, and program success, provided adequate resources and investments are made. The integration of TB services into general PHC and community health strategies can enhance awareness, education, screening, and case-finding for TB in children and adolescents.
